title: [NAME] Fixes the Nest
story:
One evening, [NAME] went out to the barn to check on the animals before bed.

The barn was warm inside. It smelled like hay and the slow breathing of large animals. The two goats were in their pen. The old tabby cat was curled on a feed sack in the corner.

But near the back wall, something was wrong. The wooden nesting box where the hens slept had tipped over on its side. Three hens stood on the barn floor nearby, making small worried sounds. They wanted to go to bed, but their box was in the wrong place.

[NAME] went over and looked. The box had slid off the low shelf where it usually sat.

"I can fix that," said [NAME].

[NAME] picked the box up and set it back on the shelf, making sure both ends were flat and steady. The straw inside had spilled, so [NAME] carried back two big armfuls of fresh straw from the pile in the corner and packed it into the box, pressing a small hollow in the middle the way a nest should look.

The hens watched with small bright eyes.

[NAME] stepped back.

One hen walked over, looked at the box, and stepped in. She turned around once and settled down. The other two followed, tucking in beside her. Their eyes went slowly shut.

[NAME] stood in the quiet barn for a moment. The goats were still. The cat had not moved. Everything was as it should be.

Then [NAME] turned off the barn light and walked back to the house. The night air was cool on [NAME]'s face. The first stars were just coming out.

[NAME] sat by the kitchen window and thought about the hens in their warm nest. They were settled now and would sleep well, because [NAME] had noticed the box was wrong and taken the time to fix it.

That was enough.
episodeSummary: [NAME] found the hens' nesting box tipped over in the barn, set it right, and packed it with fresh straw so the three hens could settle in for the night.

title: [NAME] and the Injured Fox
story:
[NAME] had been volunteering at the wildlife center for three Saturdays in a row. The center sat at the edge of the forest and smelled like pine and old wood.

That Saturday, [NAME] arrived to find a new animal in the back room.

It was a young fox — rust-red, with a white-tipped tail and a bandaged front paw. It sat in a wire kennel against the wall, and when [NAME] came close, the fox looked up for a moment, then pressed itself into the far corner.

"She was hit by a car on the county road," said the center director. "Front leg is bruised, not broken. She needs rest and calm for a few days."

"Can I sit with her?" asked [NAME].

"Not in the kennel. But you can sit nearby and be still."

[NAME] got a low stool and placed it near the kennel — not too close — and sat down with a book. [NAME] read quietly, not talking to the fox. Just being there, making the ordinary sounds of a person nearby.

For the first few minutes, the fox stayed pressed in her corner. Her amber eyes watched [NAME] without blinking.

[NAME] turned a page.

After a while, the fox shifted. She moved toward the front of the kennel and lay down, her good paw stretched out in front of her. Her breathing slowed.

[NAME] kept reading.

When the center director came back from lunch, the fox's eyes were half closed.

"You did something right," said the director quietly.

"I just sat still," said [NAME].

"That's exactly what she needed."

On the walk home, [NAME] thought about that. Sometimes helping doesn't mean doing something big. Sometimes it means being calm enough that a frightened thing can feel safe.

The fox would stay at the center for two weeks. Then she would go back to the forest and the paths she knew. But that afternoon, with [NAME] reading quietly and the fox finally resting, was a beginning.

[NAME] looked at the trees at the edge of the road on the walk home. Somewhere in there was the fox's territory. She would find her way back to it.

The evening light was gold over the fields. [NAME] walked slowly, still thinking, in no hurry to arrive.
episodeSummary: [NAME] sat quietly beside an injured fox at the wildlife center, reading aloud until the frightened fox finally lay down and rested, learning that calm presence can be its own kind of help.

title: [NAME] and the Signal Dish
story:
[NAME] was on a two-week stay at the small research outpost near the northern coast, helping a team track weather data from a satellite that passed overhead twice each day.

On the third night, the signal stopped coming through.

[NAME] went up to the rooftop deck with a flashlight and the repair kit. The air was cold and sharp and the stars were very clear. The large white dish that received the satellite signal was pointing in the wrong direction — off by several degrees.

The pivot arm had two bolts on either side. [NAME] checked them. Both had worked loose from the wind.

[NAME] found the socket wrench in the kit and tightened the first bolt, then the second. Then [NAME] looked at the small angle chart taped inside the access panel. The correct position for the satellite pass was 37 degrees. The dish had drifted to 41.

[NAME] adjusted the dish slowly, watching the readout on the small display beside the access panel. The number moved: 40 — 39 — 38 — 37.

[NAME] tightened both bolts again at the correct angle and checked the display once more. It held steady at 37.

Back inside, [NAME] told the lead researcher, Dr. Voss, what had happened.

She looked at the monitor. The signal line was coming in clean and steady.

"Good catch," she said. "The next pass is in four hours. We'll have complete data by morning."

[NAME] went to the bunk room and climbed into bed. Through the small porthole window, the dish was visible outside — still now, pointed at exactly the right piece of sky.

The outpost hummed with its equipment. Everything was in order.

[NAME] closed both eyes.
episodeSummary: [NAME] discovered that the research outpost's satellite dish had drifted off-angle in the wind, tightened the loose bolts, and corrected the position so the signal came through cleanly.

title: The Night Calibration
story:
The night shift at the Meridian Observatory started at eleven and ran until six in the morning. [NAME] had asked for it specifically, because the quietest shift was when the most careful work happened.

The job was simple on paper: run the calibration check on the secondary mirror, log the readings, report any drift to the morning team. In practice it required concentration, a steady hand on the controls, and the ability to sit alone with instruments and the dark for hours.

At midnight, [NAME] ran the first check. The secondary mirror was off — not by much, less than a millimeter — but in telescope work, fractions of millimeters meant whole features of the sky went soft and out of focus.

[NAME] opened the calibration log and compared tonight's reading against the six-month baseline. The drift matched the warm-season expansion pattern: expected, but still needing correction.

The calibration protocol had twelve steps. [NAME] followed each one in order. Adjust. Check. Log. Adjust again. The mirror moved by fractions, directed by a control panel that worked in thousandths of millimeters. It was slow work and [NAME] did not rush it.

An hour and twenty minutes later, [NAME] ran the final check. The reading sat at 0.003 millimeters off baseline — well within tolerance.

[NAME] logged the result with the timestamp and walked to the eyepiece.

The cluster of stars at the edge of the Crab Nebula came into focus sharp and clear, points of light separating cleanly from each other. The image was good. [NAME] wrote that in the log too: "Image quality confirmed. Calibration successful."

Then [NAME] made tea from the small kettle in the equipment room and sat in the observer's chair to read. Every hour, a quick check. Everything held steady.

By five in the morning the sky at the horizon had begun to lighten. [NAME] closed the dome, shut down the tracking system, and left a note on the desk for the morning team: Mirror drift corrected, all systems stable, good night.

The walk to the residence block was short. The air smelled like cold grass and stone. [NAME] looked up before going inside.

The stars were still there, just fading at the edges. They would be there again tomorrow, and the mirror would hold, and someone else would check the readings and find them good.

[NAME] went inside.
episodeSummary: [NAME] worked the night shift at an observatory, patiently calibrating a drifting secondary mirror over more than an hour until the readings were within tolerance and the star images came in sharp and clear.

title: [NAME] and the Little Hadrosaur
story:
[NAME] was walking along the river path when a small sound stopped [NAME] in place.

Behind a large fern, there was a baby hadrosaur. It was about the size of a big dog, with a wide flat nose and dark eyes. It made small sounds and turned in circles, the way animals do when they are lost.

[NAME] looked up the path. Beyond a row of big ferns was the muddy slope of the nesting hill, where the hadrosaur families lived. The baby had wandered down the path and gotten turned around.

[NAME] thought for a moment.

Then [NAME] started walking slowly up the path toward the nesting hill. Not too fast. Just a calm, steady walk.

The baby hadrosaur sniffed the air. Then it followed.

It walked behind [NAME] with its head bobbing, putting its wide feet carefully on the soft ground. [NAME] kept moving at the same pace, not looking back, not making any sudden movements.

At the top of the slope, a large female hadrosaur raised her head and made a deep, rumbling call.

The baby ran.

It went right to her side and pressed close. The female made a softer sound. She turned her big head to look at [NAME] for a moment.

[NAME] stood still.

Then [NAME] turned and walked back down the slope to the river path.

The sun was low and orange over the hills. The hadrosaur family was quiet on the hill above. The baby was home.

[NAME] walked on along the river path, happy with how it had all worked out.
episodeSummary: [NAME] found a lost baby hadrosaur on the river path and slowly led it back up to the nesting hill, where the mother was waiting.

title: [NAME] and the Stegosaur Nest
story:
[NAME] worked at the valley field station every summer, tracking dinosaur activity in the lowlands. It was patient, careful work, and [NAME] had learned to do it well.

One morning in late August, [NAME] found a problem.

Three stegosaur nests at the south end of the valley had been visited by scavengers overnight. Two were empty — the eggs already gone. The third nest, tucked under a rock overhang, still had four eggs. But the mother stegosaur had not been seen for two days. The tracker data showed she had moved to the north water crossing and had not returned.

[NAME] brought the report to Dr. Okonkwo, who ran the station.

"The eggs are still good," said [NAME]. "The nest is covered from above, but the sides are open. I want to build a screen — flat rocks stacked along the exposed side, enough to block access without disturbing the nest."

Dr. Okonkwo studied the diagram [NAME] had sketched. "Do it," she said. "Don't touch the eggs. Be careful on that hillside."

[NAME] packed a bag and spent the morning choosing flat rocks from the dry creek bed below the hill. They had to be the right size — too small and they would shift; too large and they would be impossible to carry up the slope alone.

Three trips.

At the nest, [NAME] stacked the rocks in a low curved wall along the open side, fitting each one tightly against the next. The eggs were undisturbed. [NAME] noted their condition in the field log — four eggs, shells intact, no new damage.

On the way back to the station, [NAME] set a camera trap at the bottom of the slope.

That evening, the camera recorded the mother stegosaur returning to the nest just after dark. She circled it twice, examined the rock wall, and then settled beside her eggs.

Dr. Okonkwo showed the image to [NAME] at breakfast.

"She came back," said [NAME].

"She did. And because the nest was still intact, the eggs were still there for her."

[NAME] looked at the picture — the large armored animal at rest beside her nest, the rock wall visible in the corner of the frame, holding exactly as it should.

Three trips up that hillside had been worth it.
episodeSummary: [NAME] found a stegosaur nest left unprotected when the mother moved away, and built a careful rock wall to shield the remaining eggs from scavengers. The mother returned that night and settled beside her nest.

title: [NAME] and the Moon Garden
story:
The map appeared on [NAME]'s desk just before bedtime, the way these things sometimes did.

It was drawn on stiff pale paper in careful lines, showing a winding path through a garden [NAME] had never visited. The path ended at a gate marked with a half-moon. At the bottom of the map, in small neat handwriting: Deliver the blue parcel. The gate opens after moonrise.

There was a blue parcel on the desk beside the map. It was tied with plain string and not very heavy.

[NAME] tucked the parcel under one arm, picked up the map, and went out.

The moon garden was at the edge of the old park. [NAME] had passed the iron gate there many times and never seen it open. Tonight it stood slightly ajar, and a path beyond was lit by small paper lanterns on stakes.

[NAME] followed the path. It curved left past a tall hedge of rosemary, then right past a stone wall where pale flowers grew in long rows.

At the end of the path was a small stone building no larger than a garden shed. A woman stood outside holding a lamp. She had white hair and muddy gardening gloves.

"You found it," she said.

[NAME] handed her the parcel.

She untied the string and opened it carefully. Inside was a small glass bottle with a cork stopper. The liquid inside was deep blue, the color of sky just before full dark.

"Midnight forget-me-not extract," she said. "I've been waiting three weeks. Thank you."

She put it safely in her coat pocket.

"What does it do?" asked [NAME].

"It helps certain plants bloom in the dark," she said. "Come back in the spring and I'll show you."

[NAME] walked back along the lantern path and through the gate. It closed quietly behind [NAME].

The moon was high and clear. The path home was easy to find.

The parcel had reached the right person. That was the job, and it was done.
episodeSummary: [NAME] followed a map to a moon garden and delivered a blue parcel containing a rare night-blooming plant extract to a gardener who had been waiting three weeks for it.

title: The Dream Workshop
story:
[NAME] had worked at the Dream Workshop for two seasons on the late shift, which ran from ten in the evening until the last commission was packed and loaded.

The workshop sat at the end of a lane behind the old mill. From the outside it looked unremarkable. Inside, it was larger than it appeared, with a long workbench running the full length of one wall and shelves packed with materials: compressed harbor fog in glass jars, tide-sound cloth rolled in bolts, wind collected from specific altitudes and stored in sealed copper canisters.

Each dream had to be assembled precisely. A dream done wrong would not break — it would simply arrive flat and thin, like a story with no feeling in it.

That night, [NAME] found a note from Hester, the senior assembler, pinned to the bench.

Priority commission — must go out by midnight. A child named Sola in the coastal district, age eight, requested an ocean dream with a boat she can steer herself. Two previous versions came back incomplete. Get it right. All materials on the bench.

[NAME] read the two return reports carefully.

The first version had used too little fog — the ocean had no sense of distance, no depth. The second had used too much tide-sound cloth — the sound overwhelmed everything else and the steering wheel had no room to work.

[NAME] made a plan before touching anything.

The fog went in first, measured carefully — enough to suggest distance without obscuring the foreground. The blue glass came next, laid in thin overlapping layers, each one darker toward the center where the water ran deep. The tide-sound cloth was cut to three-quarters of the standard length, which meant the sound would be background, not foreground — the kind that becomes ordinary after a few moments, like the sound of a room you know well.

The steering wheel went in last, positioned at the bow so it would be in Sola's hands the moment the dream began.

[NAME] sat back and looked at the whole thing.

Something was still missing.

[NAME] read the commission again. A boat she can steer herself. The previous versions had the boat, the wheel, the ocean. But a boat you can steer needs somewhere to go.

[NAME] went to the materials cabinet and found a small piece of coastal island geography — not a specific island, just the feeling of one. A shape in the distance, approachable, with a harbor entrance. [NAME] mounted it at the far edge of the dream, behind three thin layers of fog so it would appear slowly as the boat got closer.

Now there was something to sail toward.

[NAME] wrapped the commission carefully, wrote Sola's address on the front, and set it in the outgoing rack. It was eleven forty-two.

Cleaning up, [NAME] wrote a brief report: Third version for Sola — corrected fog, reduced tide-sound, added coastal destination at horizon. Steering wheel at bow. Complete.

[NAME] stepped outside. The lane was quiet. The mill wheel turned in the dark water. The sky had clouds moving across it, the kind that make it look like something is traveling underneath them.

[NAME] thought about Sola in the coastal district, and the dream that was now packed and waiting. She would have the ocean, and a boat with a wheel that worked, and something on the horizon to sail toward.

That was what the first two attempts had missed. Not the materials. The direction.

[NAME] walked home along the lane.

The workshop light was still on behind the fogged windows. The job was done.
episodeSummary: [NAME] worked the night shift at the Dream Workshop to complete a third attempt at a commission for a child named Sola, discovering that the previous two versions had failed because they gave her a steerable boat but no destination, and adding a distant island to sail toward made the dream finally complete.

title: [NAME] and the Seal Pup
story:
[NAME] was walking along the rocky beach when [NAME] spotted something on a flat stone near the water.

It was a seal pup. Small and round, with big dark eyes and soft grey fur. It was alone on the rock, and it was making small sounds.

[NAME] stopped and sat down on a nearby stone to watch.

The pup looked at [NAME]. It made another sound.

[NAME] knew what to do. The people at the beach information board had explained it: seal mothers often leave their pups on rocks while they go to find food in the water. The pup was not lost. It was waiting. The right thing to do was to stay back and not go near.

So [NAME] sat still.

The waves came in and went out again. The pup looked at the water, then at [NAME], then at the water. It made one more small sound and then went quiet.

After a while, a large seal surfaced in the waves near the rock. She hauled herself up with a heavy, rocking motion, and the pup went right to her side.

[NAME] let out a slow breath.

The mother seal looked in [NAME]'s direction for a moment. Then she turned her attention to her pup.

[NAME] stood up quietly and walked on along the beach, away from the rocks, giving them their space.

The waves kept coming in. The cold air smelled like salt.

[NAME] felt good in a quiet way — the way you feel when you did the right thing and let everything turn out as it should.
episodeSummary: [NAME] found a seal pup alone on a rock and remembered to stay back and wait, and soon the mother surfaced from the sea and returned to her pup.

title: [NAME] and the Harbor Lights
story:
In the harbor town of Fenwick, six lanterns along the sea wall had to be lit by hand every evening in the fog season. The harbor master, Elsa, had done it every night for eleven years. But that Thursday she had a broken ankle and could not climb the stone steps.

[NAME] volunteered.

Elsa sat at her kitchen table and gave careful instructions. Each lantern had a glass door with a latch on the left side. The wick had to be trimmed if it was black at the tip. The oil reservoir behind the second panel needed to be at least three-quarters full. There was an oil can in the storage box below each lantern post.

"Start at the far end," said Elsa, "and work back toward the dock. That way you can see if any light is out when you look back along the wall."

[NAME] started at the far end.

The first lantern was fine. The second had a wick that needed trimming — [NAME] cut it even with the small scissors from the kit bag. The third was low on oil — [NAME] filled it carefully from the can in the storage box, being sure not to spill. The fourth and fifth were ready.

The sixth, the one nearest the dock, had a glass panel that would not latch.

[NAME] worked at it for several minutes. The hinge was stiff from salt air. [NAME] found a flat stone on the sea wall and tapped the hinge pin gently back into alignment. The latch caught.

[NAME] lit all six lanterns in order from far to near. Walking back toward the dock, [NAME] turned to look. All six were burning, steady and clear, in a line along the sea wall.

The fog was already moving in off the water. The lanterns made warm rings of light in the grey.

[NAME] went back to report to Elsa.

"All six?" she asked.

"All six," said [NAME]. "The third was low on oil and the sixth latch was stiff."

Elsa nodded. "I'll have someone look at the sixth hinge next week."

She poured two cups of tea and handed one to [NAME].

From the kitchen window, they could see the harbor wall and the fog coming in and the six lanterns doing exactly what they were supposed to do — marking the sea wall so boats could find their way in safely.

[NAME] held the warm cup and watched.
episodeSummary: [NAME] lit the six harbor lanterns for Fenwick's injured harbor master, trimming a wick, filling a low oil reservoir, and fixing a stiff latch so all six burned steadily as the fog rolled in off the water.

title: [NAME] and the Rain
story:
[NAME] was deep in the forest when the rain started.

It came quickly — first a soft sound in the high leaves, then a heavier patter as the drops worked their way down through all the layers of green.

[NAME] was not scared. [NAME] looked around for a place to wait.

There was a big tree nearby with thick bark and wide, low branches. [NAME] could duck under there.

But near the path, [NAME] noticed a small rabbit crouched under a fern, looking very wet and very still.

[NAME] went to the edge of the path and found three large fern fronds with thick stems. [NAME] broke them carefully and laid them over the rabbit's fern one at a time, building up the thatch until the lower leaves below were mostly dry.

Then [NAME] went to the big tree and stood under the wide branches.

The rain came down. [NAME] watched the rabbit under its new shelter. It did not move. Its nose twitched once. Then it tucked its face into its own chest fur and stayed very still.

After a while the rain began to slow. Then it stopped.

The forest dripped and steamed. Everything smelled clean and green.

[NAME] came out from under the tree. The rabbit looked at [NAME] from beneath the fern shelter. Then it turned and hopped away into the undergrowth.

[NAME] walked home on the damp path, boots dark with wet mud, thinking that sometimes the best thing you can do for another creature is just to make sure it has somewhere dry to sit while the rain passes.
episodeSummary: [NAME] got caught in a forest rain and built a fern shelter over a wet rabbit before waiting out the storm under a large tree.

title: [NAME] and the Rope Bridge
story:
The rope bridge across Harrow Creek had been in the forest as long as [NAME] could remember. It was narrow, with wooden plank steps and rope rails on both sides, and it swayed when you crossed it. On this side of the creek was the main trail. On the other side, the forest went on for another two miles to the bird-watching platform.

That morning, [NAME] found the bridge blocked.

Three planks in the middle section had rotted through and fallen into the creek below. Anyone trying to cross would step into nothing.

[NAME] looked at the damage carefully. The rope frame was fine. The anchor posts were solid. It was only the planks that needed replacing.

[NAME] went back to the forest steward's cabin and reported what had happened to the steward, Prue.

"I know about it," said Prue. "The planks rotted out last week. I have replacements in the workshop but haven't had time to get out there."

"I can do it," said [NAME]. "You showed me how last summer when the far end needed work."

Prue looked at [NAME] for a moment. "Take the three planks from the stack by the door. The drill and the screws are on the shelf. Take the safety rope too — tie it to the rail before you work over the gap."

[NAME] loaded everything onto the small hand cart and went back down the trail.

At the bridge, [NAME] tied the safety rope from the railing to a belt loop, then got down on the bridge frame to work. The first plank had to go in flat and even, with the grain running across the bridge so it would not split with the weather. Two screws at each end, drilled through the plank into the wooden frame below.

The first plank took the longest. The second went faster. The third faster still.

When [NAME] had finished, [NAME] walked across the entire bridge — from one side of the creek to the other and back again — testing each step. The new planks were solid. The bridge did not flex more than usual at the repaired section.

[NAME] pushed the empty cart back to Prue's cabin.

Prue walked out to the bridge at three o'clock to see the work. She crossed it herself, came back, and pressed each plank with her boot.

"Clean work," she said. "Same as last summer."

[NAME] walked back along the trail as the afternoon light went golden through the trees. The creek ran clear and cold below the bridge. The bird-watching platform on the far side was open again.

Somewhere in the forest, things were already going back and forth across that bridge, not knowing or needing to know that [NAME] had fixed it.
episodeSummary: [NAME] found three rotted planks missing from the Harrow Creek rope bridge and replaced all three using the method learned the previous summer, making the crossing safe again for everyone who used it.

title: [NAME] and the Mail Train
story:
The little mail train at Barrow Station had one small engine, two cargo cars, and a red caboose at the back. Every morning it went along the valley and delivered letters and packages to all the stations on the line.

[NAME] had been invited to help sort and load the packages for one morning.

The packages came in through the big sorting door on a cart. Each one had a station name written on it in clear, bold letters. [NAME]'s job was to read the station name on each package and put it in the right car — Barrow and Millford were car one, and everything further along the line went in car two.

[NAME] read each label carefully.

Most packages were easy to carry. One large brown box marked MILLFORD — FRAGILE was too heavy to lift alone. The train driver, a man named Otto who wore a blue cap, helped [NAME] carry that one to car one and set it down gently.

"Good careful reading," said Otto. "The fragile ones can't go on top."

[NAME] worked for an hour. When the sorting was done, all the packages were in their places. Otto went along the cars with his list and counted.

"Everything's here," he said. "Good work."

He climbed up to the engine, and a few moments later the little train's whistle made one short, cheerful sound. The train began to move along the track, out of the station and into the green morning valley.

[NAME] stood on the platform and watched until it went around the first bend and disappeared.

All those packages were on their way. Because [NAME] had read each name carefully and put every one in the right place.
episodeSummary: [NAME] sorted and loaded the morning mail packages onto the little valley train, reading each destination carefully and helping the driver with the heavy fragile ones.

title: [NAME] and the Night Ferry
story:
Every Friday night in the lake district, the supply ferry made its last run at ten o'clock, delivering goods to three small island communities that could only be reached by water.

[NAME] had worked as a cargo assistant on the ferry for most of the summer, under the direction of Greta, who had been running the route for eleven years.

The Friday [NAME] learned the most started with bad news. One of the regular crew had not shown up, which left Greta short-handed, and the manifest was heavier than usual — crates of food, two large tool boxes, and a medical supply order marked for the second island.

"You'll need to do two jobs tonight," said Greta. "Cargo loading and line handling. Can you manage?"

[NAME] had watched both enough times. "Yes," said [NAME].

Loading took longer than usual. The tool boxes were awkward — wide and heavy — and the gangplank was wet from rain earlier in the evening. [NAME] moved carefully, testing each step before shifting weight, making sure nothing was rushed.

The medical supply crate went on last, in the lowest, most central position in the hold, where it would not shift on the crossing.

They cast off ten minutes late.

The lake was still. The three island lights were visible across the dark water — one warm yellow, one white, one a pair of slow-blinking lights.

At the first island, [NAME] threw the mooring line, wrapped it around the dock cleat, and held it taut while Greta supervised the offload. At the second island, the medical crate came off first.

A woman in a heavy jacket was waiting on the dock.

"That's for the clinic," she said, taking hold of one end.

"Safe and dry," said [NAME].

She nodded and walked away quickly toward the clinic building at the top of the dock steps. [NAME] watched her go, thinking about whoever at the clinic was waiting for whatever was in that crate.

The third island was the smallest — a few houses, a storage shed, a dock with a lamp on a post. They finished there at twenty minutes past midnight.

On the return crossing, Greta poured two cups of coffee from a thermos and handed one to [NAME] without saying anything.

[NAME] held the warm cup and looked back at the three islands, dark behind them now, their work done for another week.

The lake was very quiet. The ferry engine made its steady sound.
episodeSummary: [NAME] took on two jobs during a short-handed night supply ferry run, loading heavy awkward cargo carefully, handling mooring lines at each island, and making sure a medical crate reached the island clinic safely.

title: [NAME] Waits for Bea
story:
[NAME] and Bea always walked to the park together on Saturday mornings. They met at the corner of Maple Street every week at nine o'clock.

This Saturday, [NAME] arrived at the corner and Bea was not there.

[NAME] waited.

Five minutes went by. Then ten.

[NAME] sat down on the low stone wall at the corner. Some children went past on bikes. A dog walked by with its owner. A cloud covered the sun for a moment, then moved on.

[NAME] kept waiting.

Then [NAME] heard running feet on the pavement.

"I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I'm sorry," said Bea, arriving at the corner out of breath. Her shoes were on the wrong feet and her hair was sticking up on one side.

"I couldn't find my shoes," Bea said. "Both of them. First I found one, then I couldn't find the other one. It was under my bed."

"I waited," said [NAME].

Bea looked at [NAME]'s face to see if [NAME] was cross.

[NAME] was not cross. "I knew you were coming," said [NAME].

They walked to the park together. Bea's shoes were still on the wrong feet and she didn't notice for another hour.

At the park they went down the slide and looked for beetles under the big flat stone near the fence and sat on the swings until it was time for lunch.

It was a good morning, the same as always, just starting a little later than usual.

On the way home, Bea said, "Thank you for waiting."

"Of course," said [NAME].
episodeSummary: [NAME] waited patiently at the corner for Bea, who was late because she lost her shoes, and they went to the park together just as they always did.

title: [NAME]'s Map for Marlo
story:
Marlo had been home sick for nine days. [NAME] counted — two days of fever, then a week of a cough that made Marlo too tired to do much of anything.

At school the seat next to [NAME] was empty. At lunch [NAME] sat with other people but kept noticing the gap. Marlo would have had strong opinions about the Tuesday soup.

On the ninth day, [NAME] decided to make something.

Marlo liked maps. Not maps of real places, but invented ones — imaginary countries with impossible coastlines and mountain ranges that curved the wrong way. Maps with legends that listed things like: here be ordinary turnips, and road closed due to arguing hedgehogs.

[NAME] got out a large sheet of cream paper and a set of fine-tipped drawing pens.

It took three evenings.

[NAME] drew a country the shape of a dinner plate, with a long ragged coast and two inland lakes connected by a winding canal. There was a city in the north called Marlo's Landing, and a road leading south through a forest called the Bickering Wood, and a mountain range labeled the Slightly Unreasonable Peaks. The map legend had fourteen entries, including suspected dragon (friendly) and excellent soup, no questions asked.

[NAME] spent the third evening on the border — a careful double line with small drawings in the four corners: a sleeping cat, a surprised turnip, a hedgehog reading a newspaper upside down, and a very small boat tied to a dock for no apparent reason.

On the tenth morning, Marlo came back to school.

[NAME] put the map — rolled up and tied with a piece of kitchen string — on Marlo's desk before class started, then sat down and pretended to be reading.

Marlo arrived and found it. Marlo unrolled it slowly and looked at it for a long time without saying anything.

"Did you make this?" Marlo asked.

"Over three evenings," said [NAME].

Marlo looked at the hedgehog in the corner. "It's reading upside down."

"It's a very advanced hedgehog," said [NAME].

Marlo laughed. It was the first time in more than a week, and it was a good sound.

Marlo put the map carefully back in its roll and kept it on the desk for the rest of the morning, like something that needed to be nearby.
episodeSummary: [NAME] spent three evenings drawing an elaborate imaginary map — complete with impossible mountains, a friendly suspected dragon, and a hedgehog reading upside down — for Marlo, who had been home sick for nine days. When Marlo returned to school, the map made them laugh for the first time all week.

title: [NAME] and the Lantern Path
story:
[NAME] found the key on the path near the old park gate on the way home from school.

It was a small brass key with a paper tag tied to it on a loop of string. The tag said, in careful handwriting: For the lantern keeper. Gate 3.

[NAME] looked at the key. The park had three gates — the main one by the road, the one near the pond, and the old one at the back that was usually locked.

The back gate had a new padlock on it.

The key fit.

[NAME] pushed the gate open and found a narrow path running along the outside of the park wall. Every thirty feet or so there was an unlit lantern on a short wooden post, each one with a small hinged door and a wick inside.

At the far end of the path was a flat wooden box with a tin of matches and a folded note. The note said: Please light each lantern in order, starting from the gate. Leave the key in this box when you are done.

[NAME] went back to the first lantern, opened the small door, and lit the wick. Then the second. Then the third.

The path curved as [NAME] walked, and at each new lantern [NAME] could look back and see the ones already burning behind.

Seven lanterns in total.

After lighting the last one, [NAME] walked back to the box at the end of the path and left the key inside.

Walking home through the park, [NAME] could see the light from the lanterns coming through small gaps in the old wall — warm patches against the evening air.

Someone had planned for those lanterns to be lit. Someone had trusted that the right person would find the key.

[NAME] went home as the sky turned dark, feeling like that trust had been placed correctly.
episodeSummary: [NAME] found a key on a park path with a note asking the finder to light seven lanterns along a hidden path, followed the instructions carefully, and left the key in the box as asked.

title: [NAME] and the Forest Survey
story:
The assignment came from the District Land Office: walk the eastern boundary of Harrow Forest, locate all the boundary posts, note any that were missing or damaged, record the GPS coordinates of each one, and file a report before the end of the season.

[NAME] had done three smaller surveys that summer. This one was fourteen kilometers of boundary through dense undergrowth, and [NAME] was doing it alone.

[NAME] started at the northern trailhead on a Thursday morning with a full pack, good boots, and a forecast that promised a clear day. The first section went well. The boundary posts were old iron ones, painted white at the top, set every hundred meters. [NAME] logged each post's position and condition in the field notebook — good, good, surface rust only, good — and moved steadily south.

By noon, [NAME] had covered six kilometers and eaten lunch at a stream crossing where the water ran over flat brown stones.

The afternoon was harder. The undergrowth thickened past the stream, and two posts were missing — their concrete bases were still in the ground, but the iron posts had rusted through at the base and fallen. [NAME] searched the leaf litter nearby and found both of them lying nearby, too corroded to be re-set. [NAME] photographed each base, recorded the coordinates, and wrote in the log: Posts 34 and 35 — missing, bases intact, post replacement required.

At the eleventh kilometer, [NAME] found a third post that was not only missing but had a cracked concrete base shifted out of the ground by tree roots. [NAME] took photographs from three angles and noted in the log that the base itself would need to be replaced, not just the post — a bigger job, requiring equipment.

The last three kilometers ran alongside an old stone wall that marked the original boundary from before the official survey. [NAME] checked each post against the wall to confirm they matched. They did, with one exception — a post that had been placed three meters inside the line, probably corrected in a later survey. [NAME] noted it but marked it as a known discrepancy, already flagged in the previous season's report.

At the southern end of the boundary, where the forest opened onto a long flat field, [NAME] sat on the last post and wrote up the summary. Fourteen kilometers walked. Eleven posts confirmed in good condition. Two requiring post replacement. One requiring full base replacement. One known discrepancy, previously documented. All coordinates recorded.

The field was very quiet. The sky to the west had gone pale gold.

[NAME] checked the GPS battery — still thirty-eight percent — and compared the paper notes against the digital log. Everything matched.

The walk back to the trailhead took an hour. [NAME] arrived as the light went orange, loaded the gear into the truck, and drove to the Land Office in town. The clerk on duty took the report and checked it over.

"This covers all fourteen kilometers?" she asked.

"Every post," said [NAME].

She stamped it and put it in the season file.

[NAME] drove home on the long road through the valley with the windows down, smelling the forest air, thinking about the fourteen kilometers of boundary now properly documented — every post found, every problem recorded, the work complete.
episodeSummary: [NAME] completed a fourteen-kilometer solo forest boundary survey, locating all boundary posts, photographing and documenting three that needed repair, and filing a complete report with the Land Office before dark.
